toc.title: Four steps to a memory anchor

sections.title: Step 1: remember a general safety memory
Step 2: remember the details of the general memory
Step 3: remember how your body responded
Step 4: let yourself feel safety again

toc.title: "What have I been missing out on?"

blocks.p: Memory Anchors might be the most challenging to work with. While memories are technically a form of cognition, they warrant their own dedicated focus. Interestingly, if you struggle to identify memories that serve as safety anchors, your imagination can be a powerful substitute: it often produces similar effects.

Isn't it incredible how simply remembering or imagining something can shift our mood? These processes directly influence our autonomic state, shaping how prepared we feel for safety or defense. For instance, recalling a distressing memory may cause you to re-experience that sense of distress, while revisiting a pleasurable memory can evoke a renewed sense of joy and comfort.

You may not experience it again the same way or with the same intensity, but the memories will likely flavor your experience in the present moment, mirroring the past. It's almost as if our brainstem cannot discern what has happened in the past from what is currently happening. It receives memories and shifts the ANS up and down the ladder as if it were currently happening. Even thoughts of the future will trigger neuroceptive shifts.

When we remember something from the past, it's not merely a cognitive experience that stays in our brains. Our body undergoes an autonomic state shift, and we experience emotions connected to that memory. The brain sends a signal to the brainstem, which shifts our body's level of safety or danger. The brainstem doesn't seem to care what year it is or if it's getting external sensory input, internal remembered sensory input, or internal imaginary sensory input.

Let's work on identifying a memory that serves as a safety cue for your system. In my client work, I often guide people through this process, though it's common to start with imagination if accessing a specific safety memory feels challenging. Gradually, as comfort builds, we may transition to recalling a specific safety memory: if it feels appropriate and well-tolerated.

Judy recalled cutting class and going to an orange grove with her friends. Amelia remembered being with her "Auntie," who was a model for her of a safe individual and provided her with positive expectations. Joel recalled looking through the glass bottom of a boat and feeling awe. And Sabeen remembered feeling proud of herself for debate and cross country.

Each person's safety memories are unique to their own experiences. We all have different life stories; our safety memories reflect that individuality. There is no one-size-fits-all approach. The appearance and content of a safety memory can vary significantly. Be curious about what a safety memory might be for you. Try not to evaluate or reject what comes up.

But this is, of course, more difficult than it sounds. Memories require looking inward to the body's experience but also backward into the past, and it's common to encounter emotional or cognitive obstacles. Imagination might be more approachable for you. Either way, it can help to narrow your focus.
You may find it challenging to identify a specific time when you felt safe. I'll ask specific questions to help pinpoint a safe memory, person, or place in your life.

ul: Has there ever been a person with whom you felt safety, vulnerability, or trust?
Was there a teacher, mentor, or role model you felt safe with and could open up to?
Can you recall a specific location where you felt a sense of safety?
Was there a particular grade in school, a year, or an age when you felt safety?
When was the last time you experienced happiness, smiled, or felt joy and connection?
Can you recall a recent experience of feeling calm, relaxed, or at ease?
When did you last feel motivated, proud, or accomplished?
Do you remember when making eye contact with someone felt comfortable and okay?

blocks.p: These questions are more specific than just asking, "When have I felt safe?" The more narrowed questioning may prompt a specific memory. Similarly, asking, "What type of weather would make you feel calm?" differs from "Imagine a place of safety." By narrowing down the focus, it may become easier to identify a safe memory or person in your life. As you remember the specifics, you may notice those details conjure safety emotions connected to the memory.

blocks.h: Four steps to a memory anchor

blocks.h3: Step 1: remember a general safety memory

blocks.p: Start by identifying a general safety memory to serve as a top-down episodic narrative cue of safety. If you cannot identify one, use your imagination to create a scenario of safety. You could also remember a safe person in your life.

ul: Where did this memory take place?
Who else was there?

blocks.h3: Step 2: remember the details of the general memory

blocks.p: After identifying a safety memory, remember the details as best you can.

ul: What do you remember from the environment?
What time of day was it?
Was there anything else alive around you? Animals? Plants?
What did you see? What colors were there? How much light was there?
What did you hear? Was there a rhythm in what you heard? Were sounds natural or artificial? Did you hear safe voices?
What did you smell? Describe what you smelled.
What did you touch? Could you feel your clothes? Could you feel the air? Were your feet bare and touching anything? What was the temperature of what you were touching?
What did you taste? Describe what you tasted.

blocks.p: If you can't remember all of the details, that's fine. It's okay to make up the details with your imagination. For example, if you can't recall what specific fruit was growing on a tree, just make it up. The point is to provide top-down safety cues, not to write legally binding testimony about what you remember. (And on that note, please don't make up any memory details that might be significant to a legal process.)

blocks.h3: Step 3: remember how your body responded

blocks.p: Step three is to remember how your body responded emotionally and behaviorally.

ul: What emotion did you have? Did you feel calmer? More relaxed? Accomplished? Playful?
How did your breathing change? Into your belly? Chest? More relaxed? Slower?
What did your body do? Did you jump for joy? Pump your fist? Stare in awe?
Did you connect with anyone in the memory? Did you share a smile with someone? Hug or high-five them?

blocks.h3: Step 4: let yourself feel safety again

blocks.p: The final step is to allow those emotions to be present within you again. As you remember, you may feel those emotions, so let them be there. Permit yourself to feel safety. If your breath wants to go into your belly or your lips want to smile, just let it happen.

Gently welcome and hold onto those safety experiences. Yes, they originated in the past, but you can experience it now. As you practice the safety anchoring potential, stretch these moments of savoring further.

blocks.why: Memory and imagination work the same way in the body. This practice anchors through imagination, at your pace.

blocks.p: If recalling a memory is challenging, utilizing media is another option that can be beneficial. By "media," I refer to photographs, videos, and audio clips. These mediums have a powerful ability to bring memories back to life. It goes beyond just recalling the memory in your mind; now, you can see and hear it once again.

Media provides a tangible and vivid representation of your memory, making it more impactful. If you have photos stored in platforms like Google Photos or Apple Photos, or even on a hard drive, you can create a dedicated album specifically for safety memories. In this album, include only those media items that truly help you feel safe and grounded. If you're like me, memories and viewing old photos and videos is deeply anchoring but also challenging. When recalling the past, "secondary experiences" may come along with the memories.

Memory anchor "secondary experiences" may come with the memory but are not necessarily safety anchoring. These are experiences that take you a step away from being in safety. The primary focus here should be on safety, but we also need to recognize that other things will surface for you when touching upon memories.

For example, when you remember a specific safe person, you may feel connection and appreciation. But as a secondary experience, you may feel grief, loss, and loneliness as well. Likewise, suppose you remember a positive experience with your family. In that case, you may also recall or re-experience the ways you felt with them outside of the context of that specific memory. (And that may not be pleasurable.)

Don't dismiss the secondary experiences. They are real, they are valid, and they make sense in the context of your life. Please don't disrespect them by ignoring or shutting them down. Instead, recognize that secondary experiences are present. Allow them to be there compassionately but shift your focus to the safety experiences.

It may help to say hello to the secondary experiences and extend them a loving hand. Let those experiences know they are welcome to be with you by your side. Or give these experiences an image, like placing them into a beautiful container and setting them onto an imaginary shelf for later. These are experiences you can revisit later.

Another option is to stop the memory anchoring exercise, congratulate yourself for what you accomplished, and return to it when you are ready. If the secondary experiences are too much, respectfully acknowledge them, but get up and move. Use your body's activation through a movement anchor. Or busy yourself with various coping mechanisms, like cleaning or getting some work done.

If you cannot do this, identifying a different memory or using your imagination may be more helpful. Or perhaps it's best to practice the other safety anchoring potentials and then return to the memory anchors later.

After immersing yourself in the memory, take a moment to express appreciation. Appreciate that you were fortunate enough to experience that person, place, or event. Recognize the impact it had and the positive emotions it evoked. Express gratitude for the opportunity to remember and relive those moments as they continue to bring you a sense of joy, comfort, and safety, even though they may have long passed.

Appreciation suggests you have a deep anchor in the present moment, acknowledging the significance of the past and the ability to access those cherished memories in the present. By expressing gratitude for these experiences, you reinforce the positive emotions associated with your memory anchor, strengthening its impact on your present state.
Practice the four steps of memory anchoring, above.

ol: Identifying safety memories can be challenging, so narrowing down your focus may be helpful. Alternatively, you could utilize your imagination to create a scenario that brings a sense of safety.
Other feelings may arise alongside your memory anchors. Instead of judging or dismissing these feelings, observe them with curiosity and focus on the memories that evoke a sense of safety within you.
Express appreciation for the past experience and the ability to recall it in the present.

blocks.prompt: Did this provide you with any new experiences of safety?
Was this challenging for you? What about it was challenging?
Is this something you can continue to practice?
What was effective about the memory that you identified?

blocks.h: "What have I been missing out on?"

blocks.p: As you come out of a defensive state and into connection, it may feel like coming out of a fog. You are reconnecting to the external world and your inner emotions and sensations. You may experience your self, your relationships, your potential, and more, in new ways. My clients and community members have similar experiences.

Once finally connected to the present moment, they wonder what the future has for them. Their thoughts become more hopeful as they look forward to what else they may experience. But there is also grief about what they may have missed out on. There may be some anger that comes along with it.

You have every right to feel grief and even anger. It's valid. It's normal. It has a reason for being there. Recognize it for what it is as it comes up. For now, leave it be. Give it compassion and promise it you will return to it another day. For now, you'll focus on the present and what's to come soon. Along with your grief are hope and excitement. They can both exist simultaneously, so allow them as best you can.

As you notice these moments of wonderment and awe, also give them permission to exist and remain with you. Will they stay forever? I don't know. But right now, they're present. Extend a loving hand or open arms to them.

The cognition of "What have I been missing out on?" suggests some grief. But it also suggests some appreciation and deep humility. Catch it, mindfully feel it. Applaud yourself for getting to this point and encourage yourself to get to the next moment of appreciation.
